mots.sens: This term refers to exile or captivity, derived from the root 'gâlal', which means 'to roll' or 'to move'. It evokes the idea of being torn from one's country, from one's homeland, and living in a state of separation and suffering. Theologically, 'gôlâh' also symbolizes God's judgment on His people for their disobedience, but it also opens the way for restoration and hope.

This word means 'of all' or 'among all', indicating inclusion or totality. In this context, it emphasizes that Jeremiah's letter is addressed not only to an elite but to the entire exiled people, reinforcing the idea that God cares for each individual, regardless of their status. Spiritually, it reminds us that God's voice is for everyone, without distinction.

This name refers to the king of Babylon, whose name means 'the son of the god Nabu'. He is often associated with power, oppression, and divine judgment. In the context of Jeremiah, Nebuchadnezzar is the instrument through which God executed His judgment on Judah, but he also serves as a reminder that earthly authorities are under God's sovereign control.

This word means 'elevation' or 'ascent', and it can refer to a high place or a position of dignity. In the context of the letter, it evokes the idea that even in captivity, God's people are called to rise spiritually and morally. It emphasizes that even in difficult circumstances, there is an opportunity for growth and testimony.

1.epoque: This passage is set in the 6th century B.C., during the Babylonian exile, when the people of Judah were deported to Babylon following the conquest of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar.
1.passage: Jeremiah 29 is part of a letter sent to the exiles, bringing them instructions and encouragement from God through the prophet Jeremiah. This chapter is crucial for understanding how the people should live in a foreign land.
1.culture: At that time, exile was a traumatic experience for the Jewish people, who found themselves uprooted from their land and culture. The exiles had to navigate their national identity and faith in God in a hostile environment.
1.interpretation: This verse shows that even in times of exile and suffering, God does not abandon His people. He communicates with them, offering guidance and promises of hope, which underscores His faithfulness and concern for each of them.
1.commentaire: Jeremiah's letter to the exiles reminds us that God is present even in the difficult moments of our lives. He calls us to actively live out our faith, even in adverse circumstances, and to seek the good of our environment. This passage encourages us to remain steadfast in our hope and to remember that God has a plan for us, even when we are in situations we do not understand.

mots.sens: This name refers to King Jeconiah, also known as Jeconiah or Coniah. His name means 'Yahweh establishes' and he is the last king of Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. The fact that he is mentioned here underscores the importance of royalty and authorities in the context of exile, as well as God's judgment on the people for their unfaithfulness.

This term means 'queen' and represents feminine power within royalty. In the context of Jeremiah, the presence of the queen among those who are exiled indicates the total impact of deportation on the royal family and Judean society. It also highlights the vulnerability of leaders in the face of divine plans.

This word refers to eunuchs, men who have been castrated to serve in royal palaces. Their mention here highlights the role of close servants to the king and their importance in the court. Spiritually, this can symbolize total submission to divine authority, even in situations of great suffering.

This term means 'request' or 'petition', emphasizing the importance of prayer and supplication in the context of exile. It echoes the necessity for the people to seek God even in times of crisis. It reminds believers that in trials, communication with God is essential.

2.epoque: This verse is set in the early 6th century B.C., during the Babylonian exile, following the conquest of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II.
2.passage: Jeremiah 29 deals with letters sent to the exiles of Judah, urging them to live in peace and pray for the city where they find themselves, for their well-being is tied to that of the city.
2.culture: In ancient culture, royal status and eunuchs played a crucial role in politics and society, representing the continuity of dynasties despite upheavals.
2.interpretation: This passage emphasizes the reality of exile and the loss of royal privileges, but also the call to faithfulness and prayer. God remains present even in difficult moments, and He calls His people to seek their well-being.
2.commentaire: This verse reminds us that even in times of crisis and loss, God has a plan for His people. He calls us to live in peace and pray for those around us, for our well-being is linked to that of our community. As Christians, we must learn to trust God in times of uncertainty and seek His presence, even amid trials.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to send' or 'to throw'. It evokes the idea of mission or delegation, highlighting the authority of the one who sends. In this context, it sheds light on Zedekiah's responsibility as king of Judah, who sends representatives to Nebuchadnezzar, illustrating the power dynamics between nations. Spiritually, it can remind us that God sends His messengers to accomplish His purposes.

Babylon, an emblematic city of power and oppression in the Old Testament, also symbolizes exile and dispersion. In this verse, Babylon represents the place of captivity for the people of Judah, but also the setting where God's plans for redemption unfold. Theologically, this underscores that even in exile, God remains sovereign and active in the history of His people.

This word means 'king' and denotes supreme authority. In the context of this verse, it refers to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. This highlights the struggle for power and influence between these two kingdoms. Spiritually, it reminds us that God is the true King above all earthly authorities, and that He has ultimate control over the events of history.

3.epoque: This passage is set during the Babylonian exile, after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., when the people of Judah were deported to Babylon.
3.passage: Jeremiah chapter 29 contains letters sent to the exiles in Babylon, offering them instructions and encouragement to live in a foreign land while keeping hope in God's promise.
3.culture: In the culture of the time, sending letters and messengers was a common means of communication between kingdoms, showing the importance of diplomatic relations even in difficult times.
3.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the reality of exile and the necessity of maintaining relationships with the authorities in place, while remaining faithful to God's promises. It also reminds us that God uses even difficult situations to accomplish His plans.
3.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of living out our faith even in adverse circumstances. Like the exiles, we are called to be witnesses of God's hope in a world that is often hostile. It encourages us to pray for our leaders and seek the good of the society in which we live, while keeping our eyes fixed on divine promises.

mots.sens: This word means 'captivity' or 'exile.' It refers to the state of those who have been taken far from their homeland, often due to defeat or divine judgment. In the context of Jeremiah 29:4, it evokes not only the physical loss of the homeland but also a spiritual separation from the people of God, highlighting the need for repentance and return to Him.

This term refers to Jerusalem, the holy city, symbol of God's presence and the place of worship. Jerusalem represents the spiritual heart of Israel, and its exile to Babylon marks a tragic rupture in the relationship between God and His people. This word reminds us of the importance of the city in the history of salvation and God's desire to restore His people.

Babylon, as a city and empire, represents opposition to God and His people. In the Bible, Babylon is often associated with idolatry and debauchery. The exile to Babylon is a divine judgment, but it also serves as a context for the promise of restoration and redemption that God offers to His people.

4.epoque: This verse is set during a time of deportation, after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., when the Jewish people were taken into exile in Babylon.
4.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet conveys a message from God to the exiles, instructing them on how to live in a foreign land while keeping the hope of return. This chapter is a call to faithfulness and prayer for the prosperity of the city where they find themselves.
4.culture: In the culture of the time, exile was seen as a total loss of national and spiritual identity. The exiles had to navigate between their faith in Yahweh and the pagan practices of Babylon.
4.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that even in times of suffering and distance, God is always present and speaks to His people. It reminds us that exile is not the end, but a time of preparation for return and restoration.
4.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:4 teaches us that God is attentive to the sufferings of His people, even when He seems distant. As believers, we are called to remain faithful and to pray for our environment, even in difficult circumstances, for God has a plan of restoration for each of us.

mots.sens: This word means 'to build' or 'to construct.' It evokes the idea of creating something lasting and solid, often referring to houses or structures. In a spiritual sense, 'to build' can also allude to establishing a life based on divine principles, reflecting God's will in our existence.

The term 'gan' translates to 'garden' and refers to a cultivated space, often associated with beauty and life. In the Bible, the garden is also a symbol of God's presence and communion with Him, as seen in the Garden of Eden. Spiritually, this reminds us of the importance of cultivating our relationship with God and bearing fruit in our lives.

This word means 'to eat' and implies the idea of consuming what has been cultivated or produced. In a deeper sense, 'to eat' can symbolize the appropriation of God's blessings and the spiritual satisfaction found in Him. It invites us to recognize that everything we have comes from God and should be used for His glory.

5.epoque: This verse was spoken during the exile of the Israelites in Babylon, a time of great suffering and despair for the people of God.
5.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet conveys a message of hope to the exiles, urging them to settle down and prosper in a foreign land while remaining faithful to their spiritual identity.
5.culture: In ancient culture, building houses and planting gardens were signs of stability and prosperity, indicating that one was settling permanently in a place.
5.interpretation: This passage calls us to actively live out our faith even in difficult circumstances. It reminds us that God desires us to care for our environment and cultivate our spiritual lives, even when we are far from our promised land.
5.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of engaging in daily life while remaining rooted in our faith. By building and cultivating, we participate in God's work in our lives and in the world. It encourages us to be active witnesses of His goodness, finding ways to prosper and bear fruit, even in situations of exile or difficulty.

mots.sens: This word means 'woman' and is often used in the context of marriage and family. It evokes not only the notion of a partner but also that of a mother, thus highlighting the importance of procreation and the continuity of lineage. In this verse, it is essential as it underscores the divine command to be fruitful and build families even in exile, which has a theological significance regarding God's faithfulness to His people.

This term means 'to beget' or 'to give birth.' It carries a connotation of creation and continuity of life and is often used in the context of descent. In Jeremiah 29:6, the call to beget sons and daughters emphasizes the importance of family as a means of preserving the identity and culture of God's people, even in difficult circumstances.

This word means 'to multiply' or 'to increase.' It evokes the idea of growth and expansion, both physically and spiritually. In the context of this verse, it reminds us that even in exile, God's people are called to prosper and multiply, reflecting the divine promise of blessing and protection.

6.epoque: This passage is set during the Babylonian exile, a time when the people of Israel were uprooted and faced major challenges regarding their identity and faith.
6.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles, advising them to establish themselves and prosper in the land where they are, while maintaining their faith in God.
6.culture: In Israelite culture, family and offspring were essential for the survival and identity of the people. Marriage and procreation were seen as divine blessings.
6.interpretation: This verse reminds us that even in difficult situations, God calls His people to multiply and thrive. It highlights the importance of family as the foundation of society and faith.
6.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:6 teaches us that even in adversity, we are called to build lives and families. It encourages us to invest in our relationships and to see God's blessing in growth and multiplication, both spiritually and physically. As believers, we must commit to passing on our faith and values to future generations.

mots.sens: The word 'shalom' means peace, but it also encompasses concepts of well-being, harmony, and prosperity. It is derived from the root 'shalam', which means to complete or make whole. In this verse, 'shalom' emphasizes the importance of seeking collective well-being, as the happiness of the exiles is linked to that of the city, indicating a spiritual and social interconnectedness.

The verb 'baqash' means to seek or ask diligently. This term implies an active and intentional action, suggesting that believers must actively engage in prayer and actions for the good of their community. It highlights the responsibility of believers towards their environment, seeking to positively influence their context.

The word 'ir' means city, but it also represents a place of gathering and community life. In the context of exile, it reminds us that even in difficult circumstances, believers should invest in their community. It underscores the idea that God cares about the places where His servants live and that they should be agents of transformation.

7.epoque: This verse was written during the Babylonian exile, a period when the people of Israel were deported and faced major spiritual and social challenges.
7.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet conveys a message from God to the exiles, advising them to settle into their new reality while keeping hope for a return. This chapter addresses the themes of hope and responsibility in adversity.
7.culture: At that time, cities were centers of culture and community life, and the prosperity of a city was often linked to the prosperity of its inhabitants. The exiles were called to integrate and positively influence their environment.
7.interpretation: This passage teaches us that the well-being of believers is closely tied to that of their community. By praying for the city and seeking its good, the exiles demonstrate their faith in God, who is sovereign even in difficult circumstances.
7.commentaire: This verse reminds us of our responsibility as Christians in our society. By praying and working for the good of our community, we testify to our faith and commitment to God. Let us seek to be agents of peace and transformation, for our happiness also depends on that of others.

mots.sens: This term designates a prophet, a person called by God to convey His messages. The word 'navi' is derived from the root 'naba', which means 'to prophesy'. In the context of Jeremiah 29:8, it emphasizes the importance of discerning the true messages of God from false prophets, highlighting the believer's responsibility to seek divine truth.

This word means 'to dream' or 'to have visions'. It is often associated with divine revelations, but here it is used to refer to those who claim to have visions from God without foundation. This warns against spiritual illusions and the importance of relying on the word of God rather than on subjective experiences.

This term means 'lie' or 'deception'. It evokes the false representation of divine truth by ill-intentioned individuals. In this verse, it reminds believers to be wary of teachings that are not in accordance with God's revelation, emphasizing the necessity of spiritual vigilance.

8.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, a time when the people of Israel felt desperate and vulnerable, seeking answers to their difficult situation.
8.passage: Jeremiah 29:8 is part of a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles in Babylon, advising them not to be influenced by false prophets who promise an immediate return to Israel.
8.culture: In ancient culture, prophets and diviners played a central role in society, often seen as intermediaries between the divine and humans. This made discerning between true and false messages all the more crucial.
8.interpretation: This verse calls for caution and wisdom in listening to spiritual messages. It emphasizes that not all teachings come from God and that believers must anchor themselves in the truth revealed by Scripture.
8.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:8 reminds us of the importance of spiritual discernment in our daily lives. In a world where many voices arise, it is essential to anchor ourselves in the word of God to avoid being deceived. Let us be vigilant and seek divine truth, relying on Scripture and praying for wisdom in our spiritual choices.

mots.sens: This Hebrew verb means 'to prophesy' and implies the idea of speaking on behalf of God. It is often associated with the transmission of a divine message, whether of rebuke or encouragement. In this context, it underscores the seriousness of false prophecies, as speaking in the name of the Lord engages the spiritual responsibility of the speaker.

This term designates 'lie' or 'false statement'. It evokes not only the absence of truth but also intentional deception. In the context of this verse, it highlights the danger of erroneous teachings that can lead God's people away from revealed truth.

This word means 'peace', but it also encompasses the idea of well-being, harmony, and prosperity. In the context of Jeremiah, it is often used to describe God's promise to His people, but here it is distorted by false prophets. This underscores the importance of seeking true peace that comes from God.

9.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, when the people of Israel were deported and faced major spiritual and material challenges.
9.passage: In this chapter, Jeremiah addresses the exiles in Babylon, urging them to live in peace in their new reality while remaining faithful to God. He warns against false prophets who promise things contrary to God's will.
9.culture: At that time, prophecy was a common means of divine communication, and many false prophets emerged, promising comforting messages that contradicted God's judgment on His people.
9.interpretation: This verse reminds us that not everyone who claims to speak for God necessarily does so. False prophets may seduce with promises of peace and prosperity, but it is essential to discern the truth of God's word.
9.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of truth in our walk with God. We must be vigilant against teachings that seem appealing but are not grounded in biblical revelation. By remaining anchored in the word of God, we can avoid the traps of false teachings and live in the authentic peace that only God can offer.

mots.sens: The term 'Bavel' refers to the city of Babylon, a symbol of oppression and exile for the people of Israel. Its etymology is linked to confusion and mixing, reflecting divine judgment on nations that oppose God. Spiritually, Babylon represents the systems of the world that stray from divine will, and its mention here underscores the promise of restoration despite adversity.

The word 'Shavout' means 'return' or 'restoration'. In the context of Jeremiah 29:10, it evokes God's promise to bring His people back to their land after a period of exile. This term is filled with hope and redemption, emphasizing God's faithfulness to His promises, even in moments of despair.

The verb 'Zakar' means 'to remember' or 'to have in mind'. In this verse, it indicates that God does not forget His people, even when they go through trials. The theological significance of this word is immense, as it highlights God's constancy in His promises and His commitment to those who are faithful to Him.

The word 'Davar' means 'word' or 'promise'. In the context of Jeremiah 29:10, it refers to the word of God that is always fulfilled. This emphasizes the authority and power of the divine word, which never returns to Him without accomplishing what it was sent for.

10.epoque: The verse is set during the Babylonian exile, a period of suffering and despair for the people of Israel, who were deported to Babylon in 586 B.C.
10.passage: This passage is part of a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles, announcing to them that their stay in Babylon would last seventy years, but that God had a plan for their restoration.
10.culture: In the culture of the time, exile was seen as divine punishment, but also as an opportunity for repentance and return to God. The exiles had to navigate between their national identity and their faith in Yahweh.
10.interpretation: This verse reminds us that even in the darkest moments, God remembers His people and has a plan for redemption. The promise of return to Jerusalem is an assurance of God's unwavering love and faithfulness to His promises.
10.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:10 teaches us that trials are not a sign of God's abandonment, but rather a phase in the divine plan. As believers, we can be encouraged by the certainty that God remembers us and has a hopeful future for each of us. This verse calls us to trust in God's faithfulness, even when circumstances seem desperate.

mots.sens: This term refers to thoughts, plans, or intentions. It comes from the root 'חָשַׁב' which means 'to think' or 'to calculate'. In the context of Jeremiah 29:11, it emphasizes that God has thoughtful and intentional plans for His people, which testifies to His sovereignty and love. Spiritually, this reminds us that our lives are not the result of chance, but are guided by a divine purpose.

This word means 'peace', but it also encompasses notions of well-being, prosperity, and harmony. Its root evokes the idea of completeness and wholeness. In this verse, 'plans for peace' indicates that God's intentions for His people are positive and beneficial, thus reinforcing the idea that divine peace is a state of spiritual and relational fullness.

This term means 'hope' and comes from the root 'קָוָה' which means 'to wait' or 'to expect'. In Jeremiah 29:11, it emphasizes that God's plans are not limited to a mere future, but carry a promise of hope. This reminds us that our faith in God offers us a perspective of the future, even in difficult times.

11.epoque: This passage was written during the exile of Judah in Babylon, a time of great distress and despair for the people of Israel.
11.passage: Jeremiah 29 contains a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles, reminding them that despite their difficult situation, God has plans for them and encourages them to settle down and prosper in their new reality.
11.culture: In Hebrew culture, the notion of peace (shalom) and hope (tiqvah) is central, reflecting a holistic view of life where God is active in the destiny of His people.
11.interpretation: This verse affirms that God is aware of His people's circumstances and has benevolent intentions for them. It reminds us that even in adversity, we can trust in a promising future that God has prepared for us.
11.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:11 encourages us to rely on the promise that God has a plan for our lives, even when we go through trials. It urges us to live with the hope and peace that only God can offer, prompting us to seek His will in every situation. As believers, we must keep in mind that our future is in His hands, allowing us to face challenges with faith and assurance.

mots.sens: This word means 'you will call upon me' and comes from the root ענה (anah), which evokes the idea of responding or calling for help. In the context of prayer, this emphasizes the importance of turning to God in times of distress. Spiritually, this reminds us that God is always listening to those who seek Him sincerely.

Translated as 'you will pray to me', this term comes from the root בקש (baqash), which means to seek or ask earnestly. This implies an active quest for God's presence and His will. Theologically, this emphasizes that prayer is not just a request, but a search for communion with God.

Meaning 'I will hear you', this word comes from the root שמע (shama), which means to listen or pay attention. This indicates that God does not merely hear our prayers, but actively responds to those made in faith. This reinforces our confidence in God's faithfulness to meet our needs.

12.epoque: This passage was written during the Babylonian exile, a time of suffering and despair for the people of Israel, who felt abandoned by God.
12.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet conveys a message of hope to the exiles, assuring them that God has a plan for them, even in the midst of their captivity. This verse emphasizes the importance of prayer and trust in God.
12.culture: In Israelite culture, prayer was an essential practice, often accompanied by rituals and sacrifices. This reflects a personal and communal relationship with God, where divine invocation was seen as an act of faith.
12.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God is accessible and eager to hear our prayers. It encourages us to turn to Him in our times of need, promising a response to those who sincerely seek Him.
12.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:12 teaches us that prayer is a powerful means of communicating with God. By invoking His name and asking for help, we affirm our faith in His ability to intervene in our lives. This verse encourages us to persevere in prayer, knowing that God is attentive to our hearts and will respond according to His perfect will.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to seek' or 'to ask'. It implies an active and determined search, often associated with a deep desire to find something precious. In the context of Jeremiah 29:13, it evokes the idea that the quest for God must be sincere and committed, highlighting the importance of an authentic relationship with Him.

This term designates the 'heart', but in Hebrew culture, it represents not only the physical organ but also the seat of emotions, thoughts, and will. Seeking God with all one's heart means engaging fully, with passion and sincerity, in the spiritual quest, reflecting total devotion to Him.

This verb means 'to find' or 'to discover'. It implies a notion of success in the search, emphasizing that those who seek God with a sincere heart will have the promise of encountering Him. This underscores the reciprocity in the relationship between man and God, where sincere seeking leads to divine revelation.

13.epoque: This passage is set during the Babylonian exile, a period of suffering and despair for the people of Israel, who felt abandoned and distant from their land and their God.
13.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles, offering them advice and promises of restoration. This verse emphasizes the importance of seeking God even in difficult times.
13.culture: In Hebrew culture, seeking God was often associated with prayer, fasting, and studying the Scriptures. This reflects a deep desire for spiritual connection and understanding of divine will.
13.interpretation: The verse teaches that God can be found by those who seek Him with a sincere heart. This implies that closeness to God requires total commitment and a willingness to know Him intimately.
13.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God is accessible to those who seek Him earnestly and passionately. In our daily lives, it encourages us to fully engage in our relationship with Him, dedicating time to prayer and studying His Word, in order to discover His presence and direction in our lives.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to be found' or 'to be discovered'. In this context, it emphasizes the idea that God makes Himself accessible to those who sincerely seek Him. The theological implication here is that God desires to establish a relationship with His people, even in times of distress and exile.

This term refers to the return or gathering of the captives. It is often associated with restoration and forgiveness. In the context of this verse, it evokes the hope and promise of God to restore His people, which is central to the theology of redemption.

This word means 'exile' or 'captivity'. It represents the state of separation from God and the promised land. Spiritually, it symbolizes the consequences of sin, but also God's promise to bring His people back to Him, thus illustrating divine grace.

This term means 'land' or 'country'. In the biblical context, it refers to the promised land, a symbol of the covenant between God and His people. The restoration of the land is a recurring theme that underscores God's faithfulness to His promises.

14.epoque: This passage is situated in the context of the Babylonian exile, a time of great suffering for the people of Israel, who were deported from their promised land.
14.passage: Jeremiah 29 is part of the letters that the prophet Jeremiah sent to the exiles in Babylon, offering them words of hope and encouragement by promising them a return to their land.
14.culture: In Jewish culture, exile was seen as divine punishment, but also as an opportunity for repentance and return to God. The promises of restoration were therefore very significant for the exiles.
14.interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's faithfulness to His people, even in times of despair. It reminds us that God is always present and eager to restore those who sincerely seek Him, thus offering a promise of redemption.
14.commentaire: This passage encourages us to seek God in our moments of difficulty, for He can be found by those who call on Him with all their heart. The promise of restoration is a reminder that, even in our trials, God has a plan to bring us back to Him and restore us. As believers, we must maintain hope and trust in God's faithfulness, knowing that He is always ready to gather and restore us.

mots.sens: This word means 'prophet'. It designates a person chosen by God to convey His messages to the people. In the context of Jeremiah 29:15, it underscores the divine responsibility to communicate the truth, even in difficult situations. The presence of prophets in Babylon reminds us that God never abandons His people, even in exile.

Babel, or Babylon, is the name of a city symbolizing exile and oppression. Historically, Babylon represents the pagan power that opposes God. In this verse, it evokes a place of suffering and despair, but also a context where God continues to act and speak to His people.

15.epoque: This verse is set during the Babylonian exile, a period when the people of Israel were deported to Babylon after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.
15.passage: Jeremiah 29 deals with the letters sent by the prophet Jeremiah to the exiles in Babylon, advising them to settle down and prosper in that land while keeping the hope of a return.
15.culture: In the culture of the time, prophets played a crucial role as mediators between God and the people. The exiles sought signs of hope and divine messages, even in a hostile environment.
15.interpretation: The exiles' assertion that God raised up prophets in Babylon shows their desire for spiritual reassurance. It also reveals a misunderstanding of the true nature of prophecy, which is not limited to messages of comfort but also includes calls to repentance and faithfulness.
15.commentaire: This verse reminds us that even in the darkest moments of our lives, God continues to speak and act. It is essential to remain attentive to the prophetic voices around us and to discern divine truth amidst lies. As believers, we must seek to understand God's will, even when circumstances seem unfavorable.

mots.sens: This word means 'king' and denotes sovereign authority. It is derived from the root 'm-l-k', which implies reign and governance. In this context, it emphasizes the importance of David's kingship, which is a symbol of the divine promise and the continuity of the people of Israel, even in times of crisis.

This term means 'city' and evokes a place of gathering and protection for the people. It is often associated with notions of security and community. In this verse, it reminds us of the importance of Jerusalem, not only as a political capital but also as a spiritual center for God's people.

This word means 'captivity' or 'exile', and it refers to the state of dispersion of the people of Israel. It is linked to the notion of separation and suffering, but also to the hope of return and redemption. In this context, it highlights the difficult situation of the exiles and the need for comfort and divine promise.

16.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, when the people of Israel were deported and suffering far from their promised land.
16.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a message to the exiles in Babylon, reminding them that God has not forgotten His people despite their difficult situation. This chapter is a letter of comfort and hope, emphasizing that even in captivity, God has plans for their future.
16.culture: At this time, kingship and the city of Jerusalem were at the heart of Israel's national and spiritual identity. The loss of the city and the king represented an existential crisis for the people.
16.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God is sovereign over all circumstances, including over leaders and nations. Even in captivity, God continues to speak and guide His people, affirming His faithfulness to His promises.
16.commentaire: This passage teaches us that even in times of trial and uncertainty, God remains present and active in our lives. It encourages us to keep hope and to remember that His plans for us are always good, even when we go through difficult periods. As believers, we must rely on this promise and seek to live in accordance with His will, even in adverse situations.

mots.sens: This word means 'sword' and often symbolizes war, violence, and divine judgment. In the biblical context, the sword is frequently used to represent the separation between the righteous and the unrighteous, and it evokes God's power to inflict punishment. Spiritually, this reminds us that God's judgment can be inevitable for those who persist in unfaithfulness.

This term means 'famine' and evokes a shortage of food, often seen as a consequence of divine judgment. Famine in the Bible is often associated with a period of desolation and need, highlighting humanity's dependence on God for sustenance. It also reminds us that spiritual abundance is essential for life, just as physical food is.

This word means 'pestilence' and refers to diseases that strike the population, often considered an act of God to punish or correct. In the biblical context, pestilence is a symbol of divine anger and the urgency to repent. It underscores the fragility of human life and the necessity to seek divine protection.

This expression means 'bad figs' and refers to fruits that are unfit for consumption. In this context, it symbolizes God's judgment on those who do not bear good fruit, that is, those who do not live according to His commandments. It reminds us that our lives must produce fruits worthy of repentance.

17.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, a period of despair for the people of Israel, who were suffering the consequences of their unfaithfulness to God.
17.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a message to the exiles, announcing to them that God is aware of their situation and that He has a plan for their future, even amid judgment.
17.culture: In ancient culture, figs were a symbol of prosperity and blessing. Bad figs symbolize desolation and judgment, which would have resonated deeply with Jeremiah's listeners.
17.interpretation: This verse underscores the seriousness of divine judgment on those who persist in sin. It reminds us that the consequences of our actions can be severe, but also that God calls for repentance and restoration.
17.commentaire: This passage teaches us that God's judgment is real and comes with serious consequences. However, it also reminds us that even in times of judgment, God has a plan of redemption for His people. This calls us to examine our own lives and ensure that we bear fruits worthy of our calling in Christ.

mots.sens: This word means 'sword' and evokes the idea of war, violence, and judgment. In the biblical context, the sword often symbolizes divine judgment and punishment. It is used to represent the separation between the righteous and the unrighteous, and here, it highlights the severity of the rebellion of God's people against His commandments.

This term means 'famine' and refers to a state of lack, deprivation, and despair. Famine is often perceived as a consequence of divine judgment, highlighting humanity's dependence on God's provision. In this verse, it serves to illustrate the extent of the punishment that the people will suffer due to their unfaithfulness.

This word designates 'pestilence' and symbolizes devastating diseases, often seen as plagues sent by God. Pestilence represents not only physical suffering but also spiritual separation from God, who is the source of all life. In the context of Jeremiah, this underscores the severity of divine judgment on a disobedient people.

This term means 'object of horror' and evokes the idea of being a source of terror or disgrace. In this verse, it is used to describe how the people will be perceived by other nations, thus highlighting the shame and dishonor that will accompany their deportation. This brings to light the consequence of their sin and the need for repentance.

18.epoque: This passage takes place in the 6th century B.C., during the Babylonian exile, a moment of crisis for the people of Israel.
18.passage: Jeremiah 29 is part of the letters sent to the exiles in Babylon, reminding them of the necessity to live in peace in a foreign land while remaining faithful to God.
18.culture: In the culture of the time, military defeat and exile were often interpreted as signs of divine anger, and the nations surrounding Israel often viewed events in a very symbolic manner.
18.interpretation: This verse underscores the seriousness of God's judgment against those who turn away from Him. It reminds us that sin has consequences not only on a spiritual level but also on social and national levels.
18.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of faithfulness to God and the dangers of disobedience. As believers, we must be aware that our actions have repercussions, not only on our personal lives but also on our community. It calls us to repentance and to seek an authentic relationship with God, even in difficult times.

mots.sens: This word means 'word' or 'thing'. In the biblical context, it represents not only a verbal statement but also the creative and authoritative power of God. The word of the Lord is living and active, and it carries the ability to transform hearts. In this verse, the refusal to listen to this divine word underscores the seriousness of disobedience and the importance of communication between God and His people.

This term designates a 'prophet', a person chosen by God to convey His message. Prophets play a crucial role in biblical history, serving as intermediaries between God and humanity. Their mission is often difficult, as it involves confronting the people with their disobedience and calling them to repentance. In this verse, the sending of God's prophets testifies to His patience and desire for reconciliation with His people.

This verb means 'to listen' or 'to hear', but it goes beyond mere hearing. In Hebrew culture, listening implies an active response and obedience. The fact that the people did not listen to God's words indicates a rupture in their relationship with Him and a neglect of His commandments. This highlights the importance of attentive listening and applying divine instructions in daily life.

19.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, when the people of Israel face the consequences of their unfaithfulness to God.
19.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles of Judah in Babylon, reminding them of the importance of remaining faithful to God despite the trials. This verse highlights the rejection of the divine messages sent by the prophets.
19.culture: At this time, divine communication was often conveyed through prophets, and the people had the obligation to respond to these calls. Listening to God's words was essential to maintaining a healthy relationship with Him.
19.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the seriousness of ignoring God's words and the refusal to listen to His messengers. It highlights the responsibility of the people to respond to the divine call and the spiritual consequences of their disobedience.
19.commentaire: God's call to listen to His word remains relevant today. We are often confronted with divine messages through the Bible, prayer, and the Christian community. Ignoring these words can lead to serious spiritual consequences. Let us be attentive to the voice of God and ready to act according to His instructions, for He desires our well-being and reconciliation with Him.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to hear' or 'to listen'. In the biblical context, it implies not only hearing but also obedience to the word of God. This concept is central to the relationship between God and His people, emphasizing the importance of actively responding to His instructions. Spiritually, it reminds us that listening to the voice of God must translate into actions that align with His will.

This term means 'word' or 'message'. It often refers to the word of God, which has the power to create, transform, and build up. In this verse, it underscores divine authority and the importance of receiving and following divine instructions. Theologically, it reminds us that the word of God is living and effective, capable of guiding believers even in difficult situations.

This word means 'exile' or 'captivity'. It evokes the state of separation from the promised land and the presence of God. In the context of Jeremiah, it represents the consequences of Israel's sin, but also an opportunity for repentance and return to God. Spiritually, it teaches us that even in trials, God remains present and desires to restore His people.

This name designates the holy city of Jerusalem, a symbol of God's presence and His covenant with Israel. Jerusalem is often seen as the place of divine revelation and worship. In this verse, it represents the origin of God's people and the place of their spiritual identity. Theologically, it reminds us that our identity in Christ is rooted in our relationship with God and His people.

20.epoque: This verse takes place during the Babylonian exile, a period when the people of Israel were deported to Babylon due to their disobedience to God.
20.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles, offering them instructions and encouragement to live in a foreign land while remaining faithful to God.
20.culture: At this time, exile was a traumatic experience for the Israelites, but it was also a moment of reflection and reevaluation of their relationship with God.
20.interpretation: This verse calls the captives to listen to the word of the Lord, emphasizing the importance of remaining attentive to His voice even in difficult circumstances. It reminds us that God never abandons His people and that He has a plan for their future.
20.commentaire: This passage teaches us that even in times of trial and exile, we must remain attentive to the word of God. As believers, we are called to seek His direction and obey His commandments, for therein lies our true freedom and restoration. Faithfulness to His word, even in adversity, is the key to living a life that honors God.

mots.sens: This name designates the king of Babylon, whose name means 'Nabu, protect the son'. As a historical figure, Nebuchadnezzar is an instrument of God's judgment against Israel for its idolatry and disobedience. Spiritually, he represents earthly authority that executes divine judgment, underscoring that even the powerful are under God's control.

This term means 'lie' or 'false statement'. It evokes deception and illusion, often associated with spiritual manipulation. In this verse, it highlights the seriousness of false prophecy, bringing to light the necessity of discernment and truth in communicating God's word.

This verb means 'to give' or 'to deliver'. In the context of this verse, God declares that He delivers the false prophets into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, which shows His sovereign authority over events. It also underscores divine justice, where those who deceive ultimately face the consequences of their actions.

This term means 'death' or 'peril'. In this context, it refers to the ultimate punishment for the false prophets. It illustrates the seriousness of sin and the reality of divine judgment, reminding believers that lies and disobedience have serious consequences.

21.epoque: The passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, a period when the people of Israel suffer the consequences of their unfaithfulness to God.
21.passage: This verse is part of a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles, where he warns against the false prophets who promise peace while God announces judgment.
21.culture: In the culture of the time, prophets played a crucial role as spokespersons for God, and false prophecy could lead to devastating consequences for the community.
21.interpretation: This verse highlights the seriousness of spiritual deception and God's judgment on those who claim to speak in His name without truth. It reminds us that God does not tolerate lies and that truth must be sought.
21.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of truth in our faith and testimony. As believers, we must be vigilant against teachings that are not in accordance with the word of God. This calls us to seek the truth and to be faithful messengers of the Gospel, avoiding lies that can lead us astray.

mots.sens: This term refers to a curse or an expression of disapproval. It is derived from the root 'לקח' which means 'to take'. In this context, it evokes the idea that the captives of Judah will be used as a negative example, highlighting the consequences of sin and rebellion against God. Spiritually, it reminds us that the actions of individuals can have lasting repercussions and serve as a warning for future generations.

This word means 'to burn' or 'to roast', and it is often associated with practices of judgment or severe punishment. In this verse, it refers to how Zedekiah and Ahab were punished, illustrating the seriousness of their disobedience. Theologically, this underscores the justice of God, who does not leave sin unpunished and reminds us that divine judgment is a reality for those who oppose His will.

This term means 'captivity' or 'exile', and it is central to the narrative of Jeremiah. It evokes the condition of the Jews in Babylon, symbolizing separation from their promised land and their relationship with God. Spiritually, it represents the consequences of sin that can lead to distance from God, but also the promise of redemption and return for those who repent.

Zedekiah, whose name means 'the Lord is my righteousness', was the last king of Judah before the destruction of Jerusalem. His failure to follow God's commandments led to his downfall and that of his kingdom. This underscores the importance of living in accordance with divine will, as even those who bear God's name can fall if they stray from His path.

22.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, a time of great distress for the people of Judah, after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.
22.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles of Judah in Babylon, advising them to settle and prosper in this new land while keeping hope for a return. This verse highlights the tragic consequences of disobedience to God through the example of Zedekiah and Ahab.
22.culture: In the culture of the time, curses were often used to mark disdain or judgment, and exiles were often the target of mockery due to their humiliating status. This reflects a social dynamic where narratives of punishment served as warnings to others.
22.interpretation: This verse highlights the seriousness of sin and its consequences, using historical figures to illustrate divine justice. The exiles are warned that their disobedience could lead them to a fate similar to that of Zedekiah and Ahab, thus serving as a warning for their future behavior.
22.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our choices have consequences, not only for ourselves but also for those around us. As believers, we are called to live in obedience to God, as this influences our testimony and our legacy. May this verse encourage us to seek justice and remain faithful to our calling, even in difficult circumstances.

mots.sens: This word means 'abomination' or 'infamy'. It refers to actions that are deeply reprehensible in the eyes of God. In this context, it underscores the seriousness of the sins committed by the people, particularly adultery and lying, which are serious violations of divine law. Spiritually, it reminds us of the holiness of God and the importance of living according to His commandments.

This term means 'to commit adultery'. It evokes infidelity not only in marriage but also in the relationship between God and His people. In the context of Jeremiah, it symbolizes the betrayal of the people towards God by engaging in idolatrous practices. It challenges us regarding our faithfulness to God and the compromises we may make in our spiritual lives.

This word means 'lie' or 'false statement'. It implies a distortion of the truth, often to deceive or manipulate. In this verse, it underscores the seriousness of speaking falsely in God's name, which leads to serious spiritual consequences. It reminds us of the importance of truth in our testimony and our relationship with God.

This term means 'witness' or 'evidence'. In the biblical context, a witness is someone who attests to the truth of an event. Here, God presents Himself as a witness to the actions of the people, which underscores His sovereignty and justice. It reminds us that God observes our actions and that we will be held accountable for our conduct.

23.epoque: The historical context of Jeremiah is set during the period of the kingdom of Judah, while the people are in exile in Babylon, facing desolation and spiritual defeat.
23.passage: This passage is found in a letter from Jeremiah to the exiles, where he reminds them of the consequences of their sins and warns them of the necessity to return to God.
23.culture: In Israelite culture, adultery and lying were serious offenses, often associated with the breaking of the covenant with God. These practices were seen not only as moral faults but also as spiritual betrayals.
23.interpretation: This verse highlights the seriousness of the sins of adultery and lying, showing that God is fully aware of the actions of His people. It emphasizes that these sins lead to inevitable consequences, both personally and collectively.
23.commentaire: This passage calls us to reflect on our own faithfulness to God and how we testify to our faith. It reminds us that our actions have repercussions, and that living in accordance with divine truth is essential for an authentic relationship with the Lord. Let us be vigilant and seek to honor God in all our actions and words.

mots.sens: This name means 'God has heard'. It evokes the notion of divine listening and response to prayer, highlighting the relationship between God and His people. In the context of Jeremiah 29:24, the name may remind us that God is attentive to the words and situations of individuals, even in times of distress.

This word designates a group or community. It can be related to the idea of gathering or community of believers. In this verse, it emphasizes the importance of community in the transmission of divine messages and the collective responsibility before God.

24.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, a time of great suffering for the people of Israel, who felt abandoned and distant from their promised land.
24.passage: Jeremiah 29 deals with the letters sent to the exiles in Babylon, advising them to settle and prosper in this new land while remaining faithful to God.
24.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, letters and messages carried considerable weight, as they were often seen as divine instructions or important revelations.
24.interpretation: The instruction given to Schemaeja underscores the importance of divine communication in times of crisis. It reminds believers that God speaks through messengers to guide His people even in adversity.
24.commentaire: This verse reminds us that God never forgets His people, even in times of trial. It is essential to listen to divine messages, as they guide us toward peace and prosperity, even in difficult circumstances. Let us be attentive to the voice of God and His instructions, for they are a source of comfort and hope.

mots.sens: This divine name, often translated as 'The LORD', evokes the idea of the Supreme Being, the Creator, and the God of the Covenant. It is associated with the notion of eternal existence and faithfulness to His people. In this verse, YHWH presents Himself as the God of hosts, emphasizing His sovereignty over all powers, both heavenly and earthly.

This term means 'army' or 'host', and it is often used to describe the heavenly forces or the armies of God. It evokes the idea of war, spiritual combat, and divine protection. In the context of Jeremiah 29:25, it underscores that God is both a warrior leader for His people and a defender against their enemies.

This word means 'letter' or 'writing', and it designates a formal message or written communication. In the context of this verse, it represents the transmission of divine instruction through an intermediary, highlighting the importance of God's communication with His people. It reminds us that God cares about the guidance and edification of His people.

This term means 'priest' and refers to those who perform religious functions, particularly in the worship of the Temple. The priests had the responsibility to convey divine instructions and lead the people in worship. In this verse, their role is crucial for understanding and applying God's messages.

25.epoque: This passage is set during the Babylonian exile, when the people of Israel are far from their promised land, facing spiritual and material challenges.
25.passage: Jeremiah 29 addresses the instructions that God gives to the exiles in Babylon, urging them to live in peace in their situation while keeping hope for the future restoration of Jerusalem.
25.culture: In ancient culture, letters were an essential means of communication, especially for conveying messages of authority. The priests played a central role in mediating between God and the people.
25.interpretation: This verse shows how God uses intermediaries to communicate His will and instructions. It reminds us that even in times of trial, God remains present and active in the lives of His people.
25.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of listening to God's messages, even in difficult circumstances. It reminds us that God has a plan for us, and that even in exile or suffering, we must seek to live in accordance with His will, remaining faithful to our calling.

mots.sens: This term refers to a 'priest', one who is consecrated to the service of God. The root of this word evokes the idea of intercession and mediation between God and the people. In this verse, the priest has a particular responsibility for discernment and protection against false prophets, highlighting the importance of doctrinal purity in worship.

This word means 'prophet', a person called by God to convey His message. The root of 'navi' implies a direct connection with the divine, and in this context, it highlights the danger of false prophets who claim to speak in God's name. This underscores the importance of truth in the proclamation of God's Word.

This term translates to 'watch' or 'guard', and it evokes the idea of vigilance and protection. In the context of the verse, it refers to the priest's responsibility to oversee the purity of teaching and religious practice. It reminds believers of the importance of keeping the faith and discerning God's truths.

26.epoque: This passage is set during a period of deportation to Babylon, where the people of Israel face spiritual challenges and foreign influences.
26.passage: Jeremiah 29 addresses God's instructions to His people in exile, reminding them to remain faithful to their identity and vocation while facing false teachings.
26.culture: At this time, Israelite culture was under Babylonian influences, and the role of prophets was crucial in maintaining the truth and purity of the faith.
26.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the need for spiritual vigilance against false teachings. The priest is called to exercise discernment to protect God's people from doctrinal errors.
26.commentaire: The role of the priest in this verse reminds us of the importance of spiritual responsibility in the Church today. Every believer is called to guard the truth and discern the voices that claim to speak in God's name. It is essential to rely on God's Word to avoid deviations and remain faithful to our calling.

mots.sens: This term refers to a prophet, a person called by God to convey His message. The word comes from the Hebrew root 'n-b', which implies the idea of 'proclaiming' or 'announcing'. In this context, it emphasizes the divine authority behind Jeremiah's words, and his role as God's spokesperson to a reluctant people.

This word means 'law' or 'instruction', and it often refers to the divine teachings revealed to the people of Israel. It comes from the Hebrew root 'y-r-h', which means 'to teach' or 'to guide'. In the context of Jeremiah, it reminds us of the importance of following God's precepts and not turning away from them, thus highlighting the spiritual responsibility of leaders.

This term means 'judgment' or 'decision', and it refers to divine justice and the social order that God establishes. It is related to the notion of right and fairness in society. In this verse, it evokes the necessity of discernment and just action in the face of false prophets who disturb the people.

27.epoque: This passage is set during the Babylonian exile, a time of great distress for the people of Israel, who felt abandoned and disoriented.
27.passage: Jeremiah chapter 29 addresses the letters sent to the exiles in Babylon, urging them to live in peace and pray for the city where they are, while reminding them of God's promise to bring them back.
27.culture: In Hebrew culture, prophecy was a central element of spiritual life, and false prophets were often figures who sowed confusion and uncertainty among the people.
27.interpretation: This verse highlights the tension between the divine truth proclaimed by Jeremiah and the resistance of authorities seeking to silence this voice. It reminds us that God uses prophets to correct and guide His people, even in times of crisis.
27.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of listening to God's voice, even when it goes against the expectations or desires of leaders. As believers, we must be attentive to biblical truths and the warnings God sends us, and not hesitate to defend God's Word in our current context.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to build' or 'to establish.' It evokes the idea of physical construction, but also spiritual, like building one's life on solid foundations. In the context of captivity, it emphasizes the importance of establishing oneself and prospering even in difficult circumstances, reflecting God's promise to restore His people.

This term refers to a 'garden' or 'orchard.' It symbolizes life, growth, and prosperity. In the context of Jeremiah 29:28, it invites enjoyment of the fruits of labor and hope for a better future, even in times of exile, reminding us of God's goodness toward His people.

This word means 'rest' or 'cessation.' In the context of captivity, it evokes the idea of taking time to rest and recharge, even in situations of suffering. It underscores the importance of inner peace and trust in God, who is sovereign over all circumstances.

28.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the Babylonian exile in the 6th century B.C., where the people of Israel find themselves deported far from their promised land.
28.passage: Jeremiah 29 deals with the instructions given to the exiles on how to live in a foreign land. The chapter encourages the people to establish themselves and prosper despite their difficult situation, while keeping hope for a return.
28.culture: At that time, it was common for conquered peoples to integrate into the culture of their oppressors. However, Jeremiah urges the Israelites not to lose their identity while adapting to their new reality.
28.interpretation: This passage reminds us that even in times of trial, God calls His people to live actively and to hope. It highlights the importance of faith and resilience, even in exile, by building meaningful lives.
28.commentaire: Jeremiah 29:28 teaches us that God has a plan for us, even in difficult moments. By building houses and planting gardens, we are called to invest in our lives and trust in God's promise to restore His people. This encourages us to fully live out our faith, to be active in our communities, and to hope in God's goodness, even when circumstances seem adverse.

mots.sens: Zephaniah is a Hebrew name meaning 'the Lord has hidden.' This name evokes divine protection and the fact that God keeps His promises. In the context of Jeremiah 29:29, it emphasizes Zephaniah's role as a priest, an intermediary between God and the people, reinforcing the idea of revelation and divine communication.

The term 'navi' refers to a prophet, a person called by God to convey His messages. The prophet is often seen as a divine spokesperson, responsible for revealing God's will to the people. In this verse, Jeremiah, as a prophet, embodies this essential function, highlighting the importance of listening to God's words.

The word 'mikhtav' means 'letter' or 'writing' and refers to a formal written document. This underscores the importance of written communication in the context of divine instructions. In this passage, the letter represents God's will conveyed to the exiles, illustrating that divine revelation is accessible and must be shared.

29.epoque: This passage takes place during the exile of Judah in Babylon, a period marked by desolation and the search for spiritual comfort.
29.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet Jeremiah sends a letter to the exiles, offering them instructions and promises of restoration. This chapter emphasizes the importance of faithfulness to God even in times of trial.
29.culture: At that time, letters were an essential means of communication, serving to convey important messages, including divine instructions. This reflects the significance of the written word in Hebrew culture.
29.interpretation: This verse highlights the role of divine communication through intermediaries like Zephaniah and Jeremiah. It emphasizes that God reveals Himself to His people, even in difficult circumstances, and that it is essential to listen to and follow His instructions.
29.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God speaks to us even in our moments of exile or difficulty. It is crucial to listen to His word and understand that He has a plan for us, even when times are tough. We must commit to reading and meditating on the Scriptures, as they contain promises and guidance for our daily lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'word,' 'thing,' or 'matter.' In the biblical context, it evokes the idea of divine communication, highlighting the power and authority of God's word. The root of this word refers to the idea of creating, establishing, or declaring, which underscores the importance of divine revelation in the lives of believers.

This term means 'God' and is often used to denote God's power and majesty. It evokes the relationship between the Creator and His creation, as well as God's supreme authority over all things. In this verse, it reminds us that it is the Lord, the sovereign God, who communicates His will to Jeremiah.

This word means 'prophet' and designates a spokesperson for God. Prophets were called to convey divine messages to the people, often in contexts of crisis or judgment. This underscores Jeremiah's responsibility as God's messenger and the importance of listening to God's voice in our lives.

30.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, a time of great distress for the people of Israel, who find themselves far from their promised land.
30.passage: Jeremiah 29 contains letters addressed to the exiles in Babylon, where God encourages His people to establish themselves and prosper in a foreign land while keeping hope for their return.
30.culture: In ancient culture, divine communication was often seen as a solemn act, and prophets played a crucial role as mediators between God and the people, bringing messages of hope or judgment.
30.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that the word of the Lord is a direct and personal revelation, indicating that God speaks to His people even in difficult moments. It reminds believers that God is always present and active, even in trials.
30.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of listening to God's voice in our lives. Even when we go through periods of uncertainty or suffering, God continues to speak and guide His people. As believers, we must be attentive to His word and open to His action in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This proper name designates an individual, possibly a false prophet. The root of this word evokes the idea of consolation or comfort, but in this context, it is twisted to mislead. This underscores the seriousness of spiritual deception and the necessity of discernment in faith.

This name means 'the Lord has heard.' It is significant in context, as it represents a prophet who claims to speak on behalf of God without authorization. This highlights the importance of authenticity in divine communication and the dangers of false assurances.

This verb means 'to prophesy' and implies a direct communication from God. In this verse, it is used to denounce false prophets who speak without being sent by God, thus emphasizing the responsibility of messengers to faithfully convey the divine message.

This term means 'trust' or 'security.' In the context of this verse, it describes the false confidence that Schemaeja inspires in the captives. This reminds believers of the importance of grounding their trust in the truth of God's Word rather than on misleading promises.

31.epoque: This passage takes place during the Babylonian exile, where the people of Israel find themselves in a situation of despair and seeking comfort.
31.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles, conveying God's instructions for their life in captivity. This verse warns against false prophets who exploit the vulnerability of the captives.
31.culture: At this time, prophecy was a central means of communication between God and His people. False prophets, by promising messages of peace, played on the desires and fears of the people.
31.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of authenticity in God's Word. False prophets may offer enticing promises, but they do not rest on divine truth. This reminds believers to always verify teachings in light of Scripture.
31.commentaire: It is crucial to discern the voice of God among the many voices that are heard today. Like the captives in Jeremiah, we must anchor ourselves in the truth of God's Word and not in promises that do not come from Him. True trust is founded on an authentic relationship with the Lord, who guides us in truth and wisdom.

mots.sens: This name means 'the Lord has heard.' It is derived from the Hebrew root שָׁמַע (shama), which implies the idea of listening and obedience. In the context of Jeremiah 29:32, this name becomes tragic, as one who is supposed to be heard by God finds himself under His judgment. This underscores the seriousness of rebellion against the Lord and the importance of listening to His voice.

This term designates a group or lineage, and it is related to the idea of comfort or consolation. In this verse, the mention of his descendants emphasizes the scope of divine judgment that extends beyond Schemaeja himself, affecting his offspring. This illustrates collective responsibility and the spiritual consequences of individual actions.

This verb means 'to burn' or 'to be angry.' It indicates an intense reaction from God in response to Schemaeja's rebellion. The Lord's anger is not arbitrary, but a just response to rebellion against His will, reminding believers of the importance of submission to God.

This word means 'good' and is often used in the Bible to describe what is pleasing in God's sight. In this verse, the fact that Schemaeja will not see the good that God will do for His people underscores the consequences of disobedience. This reminds us that divine blessing is linked to our relationship with God and our obedience to His Word.

32.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Babylonian exile, where Jeremiah prophesies to the captives of Israel. It is a period of divine judgment on the people for their sins and unfaithfulness.
32.passage: In Jeremiah 29, the prophet addresses a letter to the exiles to encourage them to live in peace in their difficult situation. Verse 32 highlights the specific judgment on Schemaeja, a false prophet who opposes God's will.
32.culture: At this time, false prophets were common, and their influence could lead the people away from the truth of God. Rebellion against the Lord was not only an individual act but also an affront to the faith community.
32.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the seriousness of rebellion against God and the consequences that follow. The promise of not seeing the good that God will do for His people serves as a warning about the importance of remaining faithful to divine truth.
32.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our relationship with God is essential to experiencing His goodness. Disobedience can deprive us of divine blessings, not only for ourselves but also for our descendants. It is crucial to listen to and obey the voice of God to fully live in His grace and favor.
